p.src: Now, who was it calling out beside the highway? It was the mountain god and the local earth god of Golden-Pocket Mountain, holding the purple-gold alms bowl and calling, “Holy monk, the food in this bowl was begged for you from a good household by the Great Sage Sun. Because you would not heed sound advice, you fell into the demon’s hands and caused the Great Sage to endure untold hardships before he could rescue you today. Come and eat before continuing on your way; do not let the Great Sage Sun’s devoted care for you go to waste.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, I owe you more than words can say, and can never thank you enough. Had I known, I would never have stepped outside the circle, and then I would not have faced this mortal peril.” Pilgrim said, “To tell you the truth, Master, it was only because you did not trust my circle that you were made to suffer another’s ring. What misery it brought you! What a pity, what a pity!” Bajie asked, “How is there another ring?” Pilgrim said, “It was all because of you, you clumsy brute with your accursed mouth and tongue! You brought this great calamity upon Master and made old Sun turn heaven and earth upside down. I summoned celestial troops, forces of water and fire, and even the Buddha’s cinnabar, yet every one of them was snared by that gleaming white ring of his. The Tathagata gave the arhats a secret hint, and they revealed the demon’s origin to old Sun. Only then could I invite Lord Lao to subdue him; it turned out to be a green ox making mischief.” On hearing this, Tripitaka was boundlessly grateful and said, “Worthy disciple, after what has happened this time, I shall certainly heed your instructions in future.”

p.src: The four of them then shared the food, which was still steaming hot. Pilgrim said, “This food has been sitting for a long time. How can it still be hot?” The earth god knelt and replied, “This humble deity knew that the Great Sage had completed his task, so I heated it only just now, ready to serve you.” They soon finished eating and put away the alms bowl. After taking leave of the earth god and the mountain god, the master mounted his horse once more, and they crossed the lofty mountain. Indeed: They cleansed care and washed the heart, returning to true awakening; they dined on wind and lodged by water as they journeyed west.

p.src: As they went on, they suddenly came upon a little river, its water limpid and clear, its cold ripples deep and still. The Tang elder reined in his horse to look. In the distance, on the far bank, he saw green willow shade hanging low, with the faint outlines of several thatched cottages showing through. Pilgrim pointed across the river and said, “Those houses over there must belong to ferrymen.” Tripitaka said, “I thought as much when I saw the place, but since there was no boat in sight, I did not dare say so.” Bajie promptly set down the luggage and shouted at the top of his voice, “Ferryman! Bring your boat over!” He called several times. Then, from beneath the willow shade, a little boat came creaking and squeaking as it was poled out, and before long it drew near their bank. The master and disciples looked closely at the little boat, and truly it was like this:

p.src: Pilgrim went up to the boat and asked, “Are you the ferryman?” The woman replied, “I am.” Pilgrim said, “Why is there no boatman, but a boatwoman poling the ferry instead?” The woman smiled faintly without answering and pulled the gangplank into place with her hand. Monk Sha carried the luggage aboard, and Pilgrim supported his master onto the gangplank and then helped him into the boat. Bajie led the white horse aboard, and they drew in the plank. The woman pushed the boat from shore and worked the oar; in the space of a moment they were across the river. When they stepped onto the western bank, the elder told Monk Sha to open the pack and take out a few coins for her. The woman made no dispute over whether it was much or little. She tied the cable to a post by the water and, smiling broadly, went straight into the village house.

p.src: Seeing how clear the water was, Tripitaka suddenly felt thirsty and told Bajie, “Take the alms bowl and scoop up some water for me to drink.” The fool said, “I was just wanting some myself.” He took the alms bowl at once, scooped up a bowlful, and handed it to his master. His master drank a little less than half, leaving more than half behind. The fool took it and drained it in one breath, then attended Tripitaka as he mounted his horse. The master and disciples found the road and headed west. Before half an hour had passed, the elder groaned from horseback, “My belly hurts.” Bajie, following behind, said, “My belly hurts a little too.” Monk Sha said, “It must be from drinking the cold water.” Before he had finished speaking, his master cried out, “It hurts terribly!” Bajie also said, “It hurts terribly!” The two of them could scarcely bear the pain, and their bellies gradually began to swell. When they felt them with their hands, there seemed to be clots of blood and lumps of flesh inside, continually heaving and writhing. Tripitaka was in great distress when suddenly they saw a village dwelling beside the road, with two bundles of straw hung from the treetop. Pilgrim said, “Master, all is well! That place over there sells wine. Let us go and beg some hot broth for you to drink. We can also ask whether anyone sells medicine, obtain a dose, and treat your bellyache.”

p.src: Tripitaka was delighted to hear this and urged the white horse onward. Before long they reached the door of the village house, where he dismounted. Outside the door they saw an old woman sitting upright on a straw stool, spinning hemp. Pilgrim stepped forward, made a courteous salutation, and said, “Granny, we are poor monks from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. My master is the imperial brother of the Tang emperor. After crossing the river and drinking its water, he began to feel pain in his belly.” The old woman laughed merrily and asked, “Which river did you drink from?” Pilgrim replied, “We drank from the Clear-Water River east of here.” The old woman smiled with delight and said, “What fun! What fun! All of you come inside, and I shall tell you about it.”

p.src: Pilgrim supported the Tang monk, while Monk Sha helped Bajie. The two moaned incessantly, their bellies thrust out; both were so racked by pain that their faces had turned yellow and their brows were knotted as they entered the thatched cottage and sat down. Pilgrim kept pleading, “Granny, please be sure to heat some broth for my master. We shall be grateful to you.” Instead of heating any broth, the old woman ran laughing into the back and called, “Come and look! Come and look!” From within, two or three women of indeterminate middle age came pattering out, and all stared at the Tang monk with mocking smiles. Pilgrim flew into a rage, gave a shout, and bared his teeth. The whole household was so frightened that they stumbled and staggered as they fled toward the rear. Pilgrim stepped forward, seized the old woman, and said, “Heat the broth at once, and I shall spare you.” Trembling, the old woman said, “Mercy, good sir! Even if I heat broth, it will do no good and cannot cure the two of their bellyache. Let me go, and I shall explain.” Pilgrim released her, and she said, “This place is the Women’s Kingdom of Western Liang. Our entire kingdom is inhabited by women, without a single man, and that is why we were so delighted to see you. The water your master drank was dangerous. That river is called the Child-and-Mother River. Outside our royal capital there is also a post station called the Male-Welcoming Lodge, and outside its gate is a Spring of Fetal Revelation. Here, only after a person has reached the age of twenty does she dare drink water from that river. After drinking it, she soon feels pain in her belly and knows that she has conceived. Three days later she goes to the waters of Fetal Revelation at the Male-Welcoming Lodge and looks into them. If two reflections appear, she will then give birth to a child. Your master drank the water of the Child-and-Mother River and has therefore conceived; before many days have passed, he too will give birth. How could hot broth possibly cure that?”

p.src: When Tripitaka heard this, his face changed with alarm. “Disciple, what are we to do about this?” Wujing twisted his waist, spread his hips, and groaned, “Mercy! We are going to bear children, but we are men—where could a birth passage possibly open? How will they ever get out?” The Pilgrim laughed. “The ancients said, ‘When a melon is ripe, it falls of itself.’ When the time comes, a hole will surely split open beneath your ribs, and the child will crawl out.” At this, Wujing trembled all over and, unable to bear the pain, cried, “It is all over! I am done for! I am dying!” Sha Monk laughed. “Second Elder Brother, stop writhing. You may twist the child-bearing bowel out of place and bring on a prenatal disorder.” The idiot grew still more frightened. With tears in his eyes, he clutched the Pilgrim and said, “Elder Brother, ask this old lady where we can find some gentle-handed midwives, and engage several of them in advance. For some time now it has been heaving fiercely in waves. These must be labor pains—it will be soon, very soon!” Sha Monk laughed again. “Since Second Elder Brother knows they are labor pains, you must not writhe about. You might squeeze the waters until they burst.”

p.src: Tripitaka groaned, “Old lady, is there a physician here? Have my disciple buy me a dose of abortifacient, so that I may expel the fetus.” The old woman said, “Even if there were medicine, it would be of no use. But on the street directly south of here stands Mount Jieyang. On the mountain is the Child-Release Cave, and inside that cave is the Miscarriage Spring. Only by drinking a mouthful of that spring water can the pregnancy be dissolved. But nowadays no one can obtain its water. Some years ago a Daoist called the Immortal of True Fulfillment came there. He renamed the Child-Release Cave the Hermitage of Assembled Immortals and took control of the Miscarriage Spring, refusing to give its water freely to anyone. Whoever seeks water must sincerely present him with betrothal silks and ceremonial gifts, a sheep, wine, and platters of fruit; only after bowing and pleading can one obtain a single bowl of water. You are mendicant monks—how could you have enough money to purchase all that? You can only endure what fate has dealt you and await the time of delivery.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim was delighted. “Old lady, how far is it from here to Mount Jieyang?” “Thirty li,” replied the old woman. “Excellent, excellent!” said the Pilgrim. “Do not worry, Master. Old Sun will fetch you some water to drink.”

p.src: Our Great Sage instructed Sha Monk, “Guard Master with the utmost care. If this family behaves rudely or tries to deceive and abuse him, use your old methods and make an ugly face to frighten them. I shall go and fetch the water.” Sha Monk obeyed. The old woman brought out a large earthenware bowl and handed it to the Pilgrim. “Take this bowl with you, and be sure to bring back plenty, so that we may keep some for emergencies.” The Pilgrim took the earthenware bowl, left the thatched cottage, and soared away on a cloud. Only then did the old woman bow toward the sky and exclaim, “Mercy! That monk can ride the clouds!” She went inside and called out the other women. They all kowtowed and bowed to the Tang Monk, addressing him as an arhat and a bodhisattva. They busied themselves boiling water and preparing food to serve the Tang Monk, of which we shall say no more.

p.src: In no time he reached the gate, where he saw an elderly Daoist sitting cross-legged upon the green turf. The Great Sage set down the earthenware bowl, stepped forward, and offered a courteous greeting. The Daoist half rose and returned the salute. “Where have you come from? What business brings you to my humble hermitage?” The Pilgrim replied, “This poor monk belongs to the imperial mission sent by the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. My master mistakenly drank water from the Mother-and-Child River, and now his belly is so painfully swollen that he can scarcely endure it. When we asked the local people, they said a fetus had formed and that there was no ordinary cure. We learned that the Miscarriage Spring in the Child-Release Cave on Mount Jieyang can dispel the pregnancy. Therefore I have come especially to pay my respects to the Immortal of True Fulfillment and ask for some spring water to save my master. May I trouble you, venerable sir, to direct me?” The Daoist laughed. “This very place is the Child-Release Cave, though it has now been renamed the Hermitage of Assembled Immortals. I am none other than the chief disciple of the lord Immortal of True Fulfillment. What is your name? Then I can announce you properly.” The Pilgrim replied, “I am Master Tang Tripitaka’s chief disciple. My humble name is Sun Wukong.” The Daoist asked, “And where are your silks, wine, and ceremonial gifts?” The Pilgrim replied, “I am merely a traveling monk seeking temporary lodging. I had no opportunity to prepare any.” The Daoist laughed. “What a fool you are! My venerable master guards the mountain spring and has never given its water away for nothing. Go back, prepare the gifts, and bring them here; then I will announce you. Otherwise, you had better leave. Do not even dream of it!” The Pilgrim said, “Personal favor carries more weight than an imperial decree. Go and tell him Old Sun’s name. He will surely do me the favor—why, he may even give me the whole well!”

p.src: On hearing this, the Daoist had no choice but to go inside and announce him. He found the True Immortal playing the qin. Only after waiting for him to finish did he say, “Master, there is a monk outside who claims to be Sun Wukong, the chief disciple of Tang Tripitaka. He seeks water from the Miscarriage Spring to save his master.” Had the True Immortal not heard this, all would have been well; but the instant he heard the name Wukong, rage rose in his heart and malice surged in his breast. He sprang up, stepped down from the qin couch, removed his plain robe, changed into Daoist garb, seized a wish-fulfilling hook, and bounded through the hermitage gate, shouting, “Where is Sun Wukong?” The Pilgrim turned his head and beheld the True Immortal’s appearance:

p.src: On seeing him, the Pilgrim pressed his palms together and bowed. “This poor monk is Sun Wukong.” The Immortal laughed. “Are you truly Sun Wukong, or merely someone using a false name?” The Pilgrim replied, “What a strange thing for you to say, sir. As the saying goes, ‘A gentleman does not change his given name when walking abroad, nor his surname when seated at home.’ I am Wukong himself. Why should there be any question of imposture?” The Immortal said, “Do you recognize me?” The Pilgrim replied, “Since turning to the true path of Buddhism and faithfully observing the monastic teaching, I have spent all my time climbing mountains and crossing rivers. I have even neglected the friends of my youth and have not had the chance to visit them, so I have not had the honor of knowing your revered countenance. Only a short while ago, when I asked a household in the countryside west of the Mother-and-Child River, they mentioned that you were the Immortal of True Fulfillment; that is how I came to know of you.” The Immortal said, “You travel your road, and I cultivate my immortality. I am Wukong himself. Why should there be any question of imposture?”

Why does the True Immortal ask about him?” The gentleman said, “He is my nephew, and I am the sworn brother of the Bull Demon King. The Great Sage grew fiercer still, his staff whirling like a torrent of shooting stars as it rained blows upon his opponent’s head. p.src: The Great Sage did not pursue him but went into the hermitage to look for water. The Daoist had already barred the hermitage gate. Holding the earthen bowl, the Great Sage rushed to the gate and kicked with all his might, smashing it open before charging inside. He saw the Daoist leaning over the well curb. When the Great Sage roared and raised his staff to strike, the Daoist fled to the rear. Only then did he find the well bucket. Just as he was about to draw water, the gentleman caught up, hooked the Great Sage’s foot with his As-You-Will Hook, and sent him sprawling face-first onto the ground. The Great Sage scrambled up and struck with his iron staff. The gentleman dodged aside and, holding his hook, said, “Let us see whether you can take my water away!” The Great Sage cursed, “Come on, come on! I shall beat you, you wretch, till you are dead!” The gentleman would not come forward to engage him; he merely guarded the well and refused to let the Great Sage draw water. Seeing that he would not move, the Great Sage brandished his iron staff with his left hand and worked the bucket with his right. No sooner had he sent the rope rumbling down than the gentleman came at him with the hook again. Unable to manage everything with one hand, the Great Sage was caught by the foot once more and yanked off balance; bucket, rope, and all fell together into the well. The Great Sage said, “What an outrageous fellow!” He rose, gripped his staff in both hands, and charged in, striking wildly at head and face. As before, the gentleman fled, not daring to meet him in battle. The Great Sage wanted to fetch the water again, but he had no bucket and feared being hooked and dragged once more. He thought to himself, “I had better go and bring a helper.”

p.src: Our splendid Great Sage turned his cloud around, went straight to the village house, and called out at the door, “Brother Sha!” Inside, Tripitaka was groaning in pain, while Zhu Bajie grunted without cease. Hearing the call, the two rejoiced and said, “Sha Wujing, Wukong is back!” Sha Wujing hurried out to meet him and asked, “Elder Brother, did you bring the water?” The Great Sage entered and related the whole affair to the Tang Monk. With tears falling, Tripitaka said, “Disciple, what are we to do now?” The Great Sage said, “I have come to ask Brother Sha to go with me. When we reach the hermitage, I shall fight that fellow, and Sha Wujing can seize the chance to fetch water and save you.” Tripitaka said, “If both of you who are well leave, who will remain to attend the two of us who are ill?” The old woman beside them said, “Venerable arhat, set your mind at ease. You do not need your disciples here; our family will naturally look after and attend you. When you arrived this morning, we truly felt affection and pity for you. Only after seeing this bodhisattva come and go on clouds and mist did we realize that you are arhats and bodhisattvas. Our family would never dare harm you again.”

p.src: Wukong barked, “You mere women—whom would you dare harm?” The old woman laughed and said, “Good sir! You were fortunate indeed to come to our house! Had you gone to the next house, you would not have escaped whole.” Bajie grunted, “What do you mean, not escape whole?” The old woman said, “There are only four or five people in our household, all advanced in years. We have long abandoned affairs of love and passion, and that is why we would not harm you. But had you gone to another house, with a large family of young and old, which of the younger women would have let you escape? They would insist on coupling with you. If you refused, they would kill you, cut all the flesh from your bodies, and make scented sachets of it.” Bajie said, “If that is so, I am in no danger. They are all sweet-smelling and fit to be made into scented sachets; but I am a rank-smelling pig, and even if they cut off my flesh it would still stink. That is why I shall come to no harm.” Wukong laughed and said, “Do not boast. Save your strength and give birth properly.” The old woman said, “Do not delay. Hurry and seek the water.” Wukong asked, “Do you have a well bucket? Lend us one to use.” The old woman immediately went to the back, brought out a well bucket, coiled up a rope, and handed them to Sha Wujing. Sha Wujing said, “Let us take two ropes, in case the well proves deep and we need them.”

p.src: Sha Wujing took the bucket and ropes, followed the Great Sage out of the village house, and flew away with him on the clouds. In less than half an hour they reached the region of Mount Jieyang. They lowered their clouds and went straight to the hermitage. The Great Sage instructed Sha Wujing, “Take the bucket and ropes and hide off to one side while I go out and challenge him. When the two of us are deep in battle, seize the chance to go inside, fetch the water, and leave at once.” Sha Wujing carefully obeyed his instructions.

p.src: The Great Sage Sun drew his iron staff, approached the gate, and shouted, “Open up! Open up!” When the gatekeeper saw him, he hurried inside to report, “Master, that Sun Wukong has come again.” The immortal flew into a rage. “That insolent monkey is outrageously ill-mannered! I had long heard that he possessed some skill, but only today have I learned that his staff is truly hard to withstand.” The Daoist said, “Master, though his powers are great, yours are no less. You are evenly matched.” The immortal said, “He defeated me in the first two bouts.” The Daoist replied, “Though he won those first two bouts, it was only through a burst of ferocity. Later, when he twice came for water, you hooked him down both times. Does that not show you are his equal? He left helplessly before, yet now he has returned. Tripitaka must be heavy with the formed fetus and complaining bitterly, leaving him no choice but to come. He is sure to resent his master for it; I guarantee that you will triumph beyond doubt.”

p.src: Meanwhile, Sha Monk carried the bucket through the gate, only to find the Daoist blocking the well. “Who are you, and how dare you come for water?” he demanded. Sha Monk set down the bucket and drew his demon-subduing treasure staff. Without answering, he struck straight at the Daoist’s head. The Daoist could not dodge in time. The blow broke his left arm, and he fell to the ground struggling for his life. Sha Monk cursed him: “I ought to beat you, vile beast, to death. Only then did Sha Monk lower the bucket into the well and draw it up brimming with water. He left the hermitage, mounted the clouds and mist, and called toward the Pilgrim, “Elder Brother, I have the water and am taking it back. Spare him! Spare him!”

p.src: Hearing him, the Great Sage at last braced his iron staff against the hook and said, “I meant to wipe you out completely, but you have not actually broken any law. Secondly, I show you mercy for the sake of your elder brother, the Bull Demon King. When I came before, you hooked me down twice, and I left without obtaining the water. This time I used the stratagem of luring the tiger away from the mountain: I tricked you into coming out to fight while sending my junior brother to fetch the water. If old Sun truly chose to display his powers against you, let alone one so-called Wish-Fulfilling True Immortal—even several more like you would all be beaten to death. From now on, whenever anyone comes for water, you must never extort or obstruct them.” But the demon immortal knew neither good nor ill. He flourished his weapon and hooked at the Great Sage’s legs. p.src: In less time than it takes to eat a meal, their bellies began twisting with pain, and their bowels rumbled three or five times. After this rumbling, the idiot could hold back no longer, and both urine and feces poured out together. Tang Monk likewise could not endure it and needed to go somewhere private to relieve himself. The Pilgrim said, “Master, by no means go out where the wind can reach you. I fear that if you catch a chill now, you may develop a postpartum illness.” The old woman immediately brought two chamber pots for them to use. In a short while, each had emptied his bowels several times. Only then did the pain cease; the swelling gradually subsided, and the clots of blood and flesh dissolved away. The old woman’s household then cooked some plain rice gruel to restore their strength. Bajie said, “Granny, my constitution is sturdy. I do not need restoring. Heat some water so that I can bathe; then I will be ready to eat the gruel.” Sha Monk said, “Second Brother, you must not bathe. A woman in postpartum confinement can fall ill from contact with water.” Bajie said, “I did not give full birth. At worst it was only a miscarriage, so what is there to fear? I merely want to wash myself clean.” So the old woman did heat some water, and the two washed their hands and feet clean. Tang Monk managed only two cups of thin gruel. Bajie ate more than ten bowls and still demanded another helping. The Pilgrim laughed. “You clumsy oaf, eat less! Do not turn your belly into a sandbag; it would look ridiculous.” Bajie said, “It is all right, all right. I am no sow, so what have I to fear?” The household then truly went to prepare and cook a meal.

Heat some water so that I can bathe; then I will be ready to eat the gruel.”
Sha Monk said, “Second Brother, you must not bathe.
A woman in postpartum confinement can fall ill from contact with water.”
Bajie said, “I did not give full birth. At worst it was only a miscarriage, so what is there to fear?
I merely want to wash myself clean.”
So the old woman did heat some water, and the two washed their hands and feet clean.
Tang Monk managed only two cups of thin gruel.
Bajie ate more than ten bowls and still demanded another helping.
The Pilgrim laughed. “You clumsy oaf, eat less! Do not turn your belly into a sandbag; it would look ridiculous.”
Bajie said, “It is all right, all right. I am no sow, so what have I to fear?”
The household then truly went to prepare and cook a meal.

p.src: The old woman said to Tang Monk, “Venerable Master, please bestow this water upon me.” The Pilgrim asked, “Idiot, do you not want any more water?” Bajie replied, “My belly no longer hurts. The fetal influence seems to have dispersed, and I feel perfectly well. Why should I drink more water?” The Pilgrim said, “Since both of them are well now, we shall give the water to your family.” The old woman thanked the Pilgrim, poured the remaining water into an earthenware jar, and buried it in the ground behind the house. She told all the young and old of the household, “This jar of water will be enough to provide for my funeral.” Everyone, young and old, rejoiced. They prepared a vegetarian meal and set out the tables and stools. Tang Monk and his disciples ate the vegetarian meal, then rested at ease for the night.
